research.adaptation: Create original content-led hook, useful teaching/comparison/story/problem, then real Salah Alarm demonstration and truthful app CTA.
Om's generatable-format example: one ayah, one linguistic insight, one share prompt, CTA at the end. Prioritized format for this batch; audio saved to Audio folder.
Om's CTA-study example: a 9-second resonant reminder with no pitch, whose comment section became the distribution engine. Model for comment-name CTA creative.
Problem-before-product shape: phone-checking first thing vs saying the waking dua first, then wudu and Fajr. Maps directly to SalaLam's phone-distraction problem and SalahLock angle.
Phone-reach habit reframed as a spiritual moment: wake, remember Allah, then dua. Same phone-distraction problem SalaLam's SalahLock addresses; teaching-first, CTA-ready.
Couple-led Fajr story where the shared wake-up is the hook and the mat scan is the turning point, keeping the comedy gentle and the prayer itself respectful.
Education-first reel where the checklist is the value and the app only appears as the on-time prompt and streak keeper, never as a shortcut to perfect prayer.
One-dhikr teaching format where the reminder is the whole video and the app is only the prompt that protects those two minutes after Fajr.
Comeback framing where the message is return, not guilt, and the app is presented only as a waking aid, with no promise about reward or forgiveness.
Family morning sequence where the order is the teaching and the app only appears as the Fajr time prompt for the household.
Long-form education piece where depth is the value; the app is only the prayer-times reference and streak tracker, not a teacher of the prayer itself.
Pet-interruption humor where the joke is the cat, never the prayer, and the app only appears as the on-time prompt that gets the owner to the mat.
Streak-joke format where humor carries the hook and the mat scan is the punchline that solves the wake-up, with no claim the streak itself is guaranteed.
Quiet reflective format where the question invites comments and the app is the unglamorous system behind the mornings that feel effortless.
Parent-child teaching story where the steps are the value and the app only appears as the family's Fajr prompt.

Evening-timing explainer; topic stretch noted: the source is a scholarly fasting-time explanation, not a routine vlog, so Evening Routine is the closest of the seven topics because it turns on Maghrib

Full-day system framing where the five prayers are the structure; topic stretch noted: the source covers the whole day, so Prayer Consistency is the closest single topic rather than Morning Routine al
Small-steps testimony where the streak survives imperfection; the app is only the tracker and prompt, with no claim that consistency guarantees any outcome.
Transformation testimony where the journey, not the endpoint, is the usable format; the app appears only as the daily prompt and streak keeper.
Reflective reframe format where the idea is the hook and the app only appears as the pause prompt, with no claim about spiritual outcomes.
Calm morning adhkar format where the routine is the value; metrics were not visible in the search snippet, so likes, comments, views and shares are recorded as null.
Parent-mirror format where the question is the hook and the app is only the household wake-up aid, with no claim about children's outcomes.
Travel morning routine where Fajr anchors an unfamiliar day; the app is only the prayer-times reference and wake-up aid on the road.
Travel morning vlog where place anchors the routine; the app appears only as the prayer-times and mosque-time reference.
Beginner Ramadan morning where honesty is the hook; the app is only the wake-up aid, with no claim about barakah or ease as outcomes.
Music-cue wake-up format where the song is the hook; the app is only the alarm that cannot be snoozed away, demonstrated by the mat scan.
Provocation format where the argument is the hook and the mat scan answers it directly, with no claim that Fajr guarantees success.
POV wait comedy where the relatable gap is the joke and the mat scan is the payoff that gets the creator to Fajr.
Outsider-reaction humor where surprise is the hook; topic stretch noted: the source reacts to the adhan, not to praying itself, so Humor is the closest of the seven topics.
Children's animation explainer where the question is the format; the app appears only as the family's prayer-times reference.
Blunt accountability format where the challenge is the hook and the make-up steps are the value; the app is only the prompt and tracker.
One-hour framing where proportion is the persuasion; the app appears only as the prayer-time prompt and the block that protects the hour, with no guaranteed outcomes.

Night-prayer education; topic stretch noted: the source teaches tahajjud and qiyam, not Fajr itself, so Fajr Waking is the closest of the seven topics because it turns on waking in the night before Fa
Couple-consistency format where togetherness is the mechanism; the app appears only as the shared prayer-times prompt.
Phone-first swap format where the replacement habit is the whole idea; the app appears only as the lock that keeps the phone closed until prayer, demonstrated, not claimed as a guarantee.
A quiet visual journey from bed to mosque makes Fajr feel peaceful rather than punishing, which is the tone a Fajr alarm creative needs.
A sleepy child who needs a parent's nudge shows the real Fajr obstacle is waking, not belief, and a family routine frame makes the alarm relatable.
A cinematic village dawn makes Fajr feel beautiful and communal, a useful contrast to the usual guilt-led Fajr creative.
A Quran-anchored 'never give up' reminder reframes missed prayers as a reason to return, not quit, which suits a streak-recovery angle.
A story where a young man almost misses Fajr and then chooses the mosque dramatises the exact snooze-versus-prayer choice.
A checklist of six common mistakes gives a clear, saveable structure, and a checklist is the easiest format to rebuild without copying the source.
Naming the focus-stealer in salah gives viewers a reason for wandering minds and a simple, memorable cure.
One surprising word-order detail in Al-Fatihah rewards slow attention, a pattern that works for short, thoughtful education reels.
A 'do not put prayer off' reminder uses urgency about tomorrow not being guaranteed, a strong but honest emotional lever.
A short hadith reminder to never abandon salah works because it is brief, authoritative, and easy to repeat.
A calm 'find peace through consistent prayer' short sells the feeling of consistency, not the obligation, which is a softer entry point.
A 'nothing stops his salah' clip uses admiration for someone who prays despite obstacles, a strong social-proof pattern.
The river-bathing analogy for five daily prayers makes return and forgiveness concrete and memorable.
Contrasting worldly worry with forgotten Fajr names the trade-off viewers actually make at night and in the morning.
The 'last call of Fajr' framing makes the adhan feel urgent and personal, not background noise.
What to do after Fajr turns the post-prayer window into a routine, which is where a streak habit can actually stick.
A kids short where a boy chooses prayer over sleep, despite a whisper to stay in bed, makes Fajr a brave choice, not a chore.
Sleeping after Isha and waking for Fajr frames the whole night as preparation, which is an evening-routine angle, with a stretch noted in the brief.
A 40-day Fajr jamaat challenge turns consistency into a public, day-counted journey, the closest format to a streak product.
A right-versus-wrong salah skit uses gentle comedy to teach, because laughter lowers defensiveness about mistakes.
A boy making sure his toy dinosaur does not miss a rakah is funny because it is sincere, and sincerity is what makes it shareable.
A POV Muslim-life reel works because viewers recognise themselves in the small, shared moments of communal prayer.
A comedy rule about saying MashaAllah when complimenting works because it is a shared social rule with a funny consequence.
A numbered comedy series with a dhikr theme uses repetition and familiarity, so viewers know the format before it starts.
A MashaAllah comedy short uses a familiar phrase as the punchline, which is easy to remake in any language or setting.
An elder brother teaching salah, with comedy, works because teaching is usually awkward and the humour makes it watchable.
A calming night ritual with a short recitation before bed gives an evening wind-down that leads naturally to a better Fajr morning.
A calm Friday reminder card shows how a soft, non-urgent hook can open a morning routine story without lecturing; for SalaLam it matters because the product moment is the next morning, not the Friday
Night-time comfort copy shows why awake-at-night moments are a strong opening for a Fajr story: the viewer is already awake, and the gap is what they do next instead of scrolling.
A one-line hope image proves a short visual line can carry a reminder; for SalaLam the lesson is to keep the hook short and put the waking mechanism, not more motivation, in the middle slides.
A direct verse warning works because it names forgetting plainly; for SalaLam it maps to the morning version of forgetting, where the phone comes first and prayer slips.
A comfort verse is useful for restart content: it lowers the shame of a missed week, which is exactly the audience a streak-based Fajr alarm needs to re-engage.
One Arabic word as the whole message shows minimal typography can outperform a paragraph; for SalaLam a one-word Fajr hook can carry a carousel that then explains the prayer-mat scan.
Friday framing plus everyday kindness shows occasion content can still point at personal consistency; for SalaLam the bridge is keeping a promise to yourself at Fajr, not only to others.
A superlative curiosity hook (shortest and strongest) earns the swipe; for SalaLam it reframes the Fajr problem as waking, not praying, since the prayer itself is short.
A handmade bead tracker proves visible progress motivates consistency; for SalaLam the phone streak is the same psychology in digital form, visible before the day starts.
Decor as a daily reminder shows environment cues work when seen every morning; for SalaLam the parallel is an alarm that requires action at the prayer mat rather than a reminder that can be ignored.
The adhan slogan as a mantra links prayer directly to success language; for SalaLam it gives a bold opening line that still needs a concrete waking mechanism behind it.
Occasion content works when it converts inspiration into a next-morning commitment; for SalaLam the useful move is setting the adhan alarm on the night of the occasion itself.

The Fajr and Isha hadith is the strongest waking hook in this batch because it names the difficulty honestly; for SalaLam it justifies leading with the mechanism, the prayer-mat scan, rather than more
Extreme minimalism shows white space and one trust line can stop a scroll; for SalaLam the contrast with a noisy snooze loop makes the same line work as an opening slide.
A five-small-habits list works because smallness, not intensity, is the promise; for SalaLam the first small habit, waking ten minutes before Fajr, is the natural product moment.
Calling framing makes the bed the antagonist and the call the invitation; for SalaLam that choice, comfort versus call, is the exact decision the prayer-mat scan is designed to force.
A step-by-step guide structure teaches before it persuades; for SalaLam the guide order (timing, preparation, then waking) keeps the product demo in its proper late place.
A Roman Urdu Friday blessing shows warmth and community tone travel across languages; for SalaLam the same blessing can open a carousel that then addresses weekday Fajr misses.
Appointed-time reassurance is a strong timing hook; for SalaLam it supports a night-before preparation message, setting the adhan alarm tonight for a prayer with a fixed time.
An answered-dua verse gives a warm, hopeful opening; for SalaLam it pairs naturally with waking for Fajr first and making dua after, rather than dua as a substitute for waking.
Gratitude plus patience pairing is a saveable morning frame; for SalaLam the first grateful action of the day, Fajr on time, turns a sentiment into a streak.
A three-beat reassurance line is memorable because of rhythm; for SalaLam the rhythm can open a carousel that then names the one morning action, prayer before scrolling.
A visual dhikr image shows stillness can be the hook; for SalaLam the calm image contrasts with a noisy morning and supports a slow, unrushed prayer after a successful wake-up.
Minimalist calligraphy proves the surah itself can be the content; for SalaLam the daybreak link in Al-Falaq connects refuge at dawn directly to Fajr timing.

A voice-first post shows audio can be the experience while the image is only a cover; for SalaLam the honest adaptation is to describe recitation, not fake audio, and pair Quran in the app with a pray

Habit-identity framing is the strongest consistency argument in this batch: you become what you repeat; for SalaLam SalahLock and the streak are the mechanism that changes what gets repeated first thi
Slow, mindful dhikr contrasts with rushed prayer; for SalaLam the lesson is to wake early enough, via the adhan alarm, that prayer itself does not have to be rushed.
A 20-slide comment-prompt carousel is the clearest comment-CTA structure in this batch: long value first, comment ask last; for SalaLam it models how to earn an ask-for-the-app-name comment without a
A 16-slide visual sequence proves images alone can carry a story; for SalaLam a visual-first reminder carousel can show dawn, phone glow, and prayer mat in sequence before any product screen appears.

A three-slide comparison format teaches a distinction cleanly, one idea per slide; for SalaLam it maps to motivation versus mechanism, the distinction that explains why more alarms alone do not fix Fa
Long-form (221s) affirmation hook: waking for Fajr as a sign of being loved. High raw likes (24.1K in one crawl; other crawls of the same ID differ, so no multiplier claimed).
Comedy pray-with-me clip. Humor hook only; the brief keeps prayer itself respectful and the joke on everyday awkwardness, not on worship.
Comedy clip titled Prayer is the key. Same guardrail as above: joke on the situation, not on salah.

Single image, not a carousel: one static list of the five prayers and their rakah counts. Useful as a reference frame, not as a slide sequence. Adaptation must not present it as a multi-slide carousel
10-slide wudu and salah steps. Source itself notes its pictures were taken from Pinterest, so credit/attribution must be preserved and the adaptation must be original, not a copy of those images.
Single image, not a carousel. A post-Fajr 20-minute routine (istighfar, dhikr, morning dua). Adaptation is a new reel, not a slide copy.

Weekly Thursday night dhikr between Maghrib and Isha at a masjid. Community/routine angle: a fixed weekly slot, not a one-off push.

Daily reminder on sabr, tawakkul, gratitude and sincere worship. High comment count for its views: the reminder invites personal reflection replies, which is the comment engine.
